stem: A parent asks how to protect a 4-month-old infant from ultraviolet exposure. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Use sunscreen as the primary protection for the infant because shade and clothing provide insufficient ultraviolet protection.
options.B: Provide brief direct midday sun exposure each day because infants younger than 6 months are less susceptible to sunburn.
options.C: Apply an adult sunscreen routinely to all exposed skin before using shade or protective clothing.
options.D: Keep the infant out of direct sunlight when possible, use shade and protective clothing, and ask the pediatrician or another clinician before applying sunscreen.

rationale: Current FDA guidance states that sunscreen is not generally recommended for infants younger than 6 months because their skin is more vulnerable to sunscreen adverse effects. The best protection is to keep infants out of direct sunlight, use shade and protective clothing when outdoors, and consult a doctor before applying sunscreen to a child younger than 6 months. Therefore D is correct. A and C make sunscreen the primary or routine first-line protection contrary to FDA guidance, while B exposes the infant during peak-intensity sunlight and falsely assumes reduced sunburn susceptibility.
educational_objective: Protect infants younger than 6 months from ultraviolet exposure primarily with shade, avoidance of direct sunlight and protective clothing, and consult a clinician before using sunscreen.
source_document_title: Should You Put Sunscreen on Infants? Not Usually; Sunscreen: How to Help Protect Your Skin from the Sun
source_version_date: Current FDA infant-sun-protection and sunscreen guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026; FDA sunscreen page reflects June 2026 monograph update
source_locator: Should You Put Sunscreen on Infants? Not Usually: FDA/AAP recommend keeping newborns and babies <6 months out of direct sunlight; shade is best protection; protective clothing/hat; check with pediatrician before sunscreen. source_claim_supported: For infants younger than 6 months, FDA recommends avoiding direct sun, using shade and protective clothing, and consulting a clinician before applying sunscreen rather than relying on sunscreen as the primary protective measure.

source_original.rationale: FDA guidance recommends keeping infants younger than 6 months out of direct sunlight, using shade and protective clothing, and consulting a pediatrician before applying sunscreen to this age group. Sunscreen is not generally recommended as the primary protection for young infants.
source_original.source_detail: For infants younger than 6 months, FDA recommends shade and protective clothing and advises consulting a pediatrician before sunscreen use. correction_summary: Retained the infant sun-protection construct and key D. Tightened the wording to current FDA guidance by using clinician consultation before sunscreen and preserving shade/protective clothing as the primary strategy; no difficulty change was needed.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current FDA infant sunscreen/sun-protection guidance; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: FDA infant sun-safety pages live-rechecked 2026-08-16, including the 2026 sunscreen-information update
audit_findings.exact_locator: FDA infant sunscreen Consumer Update and Sunscreen FAQ under infants/children
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses the age-specific FDA recommendations and does not claim sunscreen can never be used under 6 months; it directs clinician consultation before use.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because FDA does not recommend sunscreen as the primary protection for infants <6 months.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because young infants are vulnerable to sunburn and peak direct sun should be avoided.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because routine adult-sunscreen-first use is not the recommended strategy for infants <6 months.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D combines direct-sun avoidance, shade/protective clothing and clinician consultation before sunscreen for a 4-month-old.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are UV-protection strategies for the same infant age group.
audit_findings.blueprint: Health Promotion and Maintenance — infant anticipatory guidance and injury/environmental-exposure prevention.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current FDA infant sunscreen and 2026 sunscreen guidance, all alternatives, rationale, objective, age-specific wording, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN mapping. D remained uniquely correct.
